whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Tableau Architect exam for?

personas.label: Enterprise architects
personas.description: You decide how Tableau is deployed, secured and scaled across a large organisation.

personas.label: Tableau Server administrators moving up
personas.description: You run the platform today and want to own its design rather than its daily operation.

personas.label: BI platform leads
personas.description: You are responsible for analytics for the whole business, including governance and cost.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Tableau Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam is about running Tableau at scale rather than building views. It covers how the platform is deployed and sized, how data sources are governed, how security is designed including row-level access, and how to keep it fast as usage grows.
bullets: 63% to pass, about 38 correct answers out of 59. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book.
Platform knowledge. Processes, topology, sizing, high availability and upgrades.
Governance matters. Projects, permissions, certified sources and content lifecycle are heavily tested.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can design a deployment for a stated number of users, explain which processes to add when a bottleneck appears, and set up row-level security without duplicating workbooks. Aim for 75% or more on practice tests.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe an organisation's situation, such as slow dashboards at month end or a need to isolate one region's data, and ask which platform design or setting solves it.
bestWayToPass: Learn the server processes: What the VizQL, backgrounder, data engine, repository and gateway each do, and which one to scale for a given symptom.
Design security once: Row-level security on a published data source beats one workbook per audience.
Know the deployment choices: Tableau Cloud versus self-managed Server, and what each means for control, upgrades and cost.
Plan governance up front: Project structure, group-based permissions, certification and a plan for retiring stale content.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers designing and governing Tableau for an enterprise: deployment topology and sizing, published data sources, security including row-level access, performance at scale, and content governance.

keyConcepts.h2: Tableau Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Platform Topology and Processes
blocks.body: A Tableau Server deployment is made of processes with distinct jobs. The **gateway** receives requests and routes them. **VizQL** renders views, so it is what you scale when interactive dashboards are slow for many concurrent users. The **backgrounder** runs extract refreshes and subscriptions, so it is what you scale when refreshes queue or finish late. The **data engine** stores and queries extracts. The **repository** is the PostgreSQL database holding metadata, users, permissions and usage history. **Tableau Cloud** removes this work entirely at the cost of control over infrastructure and upgrade timing, which is the usual trade-off in exam scenarios.

blocks.heading: Data Source Strategy
blocks.body: At scale, the unit of governance is the **published data source**, not the workbook. One source with agreed joins, calculations and field names, reused everywhere, prevents the common failure where every team reports a different number for the same measure. **Certification** marks the trusted ones. Decide per source whether a **live connection** or an **extract** fits: extracts are fast and shield the source database but are only as current as the last refresh, while live connections are current but push load onto the source every time someone opens a view. Schedule refreshes to match how fresh the data actually needs to be.

blocks.heading: Security and Row-Level Access
blocks.body: Access has two layers. **Content permissions** decide who can see and edit workbooks and data sources, and should be granted to **groups** at the **project** level rather than user by user. **Row-level security** decides which rows a user sees inside a view, so one dashboard can serve many audiences. The usual approach is an entitlements table mapping users to the records they may see, joined to the data and filtered by the logged-in username, applied on the **published data source** so every workbook inherits it. The alternative, one workbook per region or team, multiplies maintenance and is almost always the wrong answer.

blocks.heading: Performance and Scale
blocks.body: Performance problems usually start in the data, not the hardware. Reduce extracts by filtering rows, removing unused fields and aggregating. Keep dashboards focused, since every worksheet and quick filter costs a query. Watch for very wide crosstabs and for calculations that force row-level work on large tables. Once the content is efficient, scale the platform to the symptom: more VizQL capacity for slow interactive viewing, more backgrounder capacity for queueing refreshes. For resilience, a highly available deployment runs redundant processes across several nodes so one failure does not take the platform down.

blocks.heading: Governance and Content Lifecycle
blocks.body: Governance keeps a large deployment usable. Structure **projects** to match how the business is organised, and set permissions on them by group so new content inherits sensible access. Decide who may publish and who may only view. Use **certification** so users can tell trusted sources from experiments. Plan for the lifecycle: content accumulates, and stale dashboards erode trust, so use **usage data from the repository** to find what nobody opens and retire it. Agree naming conventions, and monitor licence consumption so the platform's cost stays visible.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Tableau Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions name a symptom or a constraint. Match it to the process, setting or governance control that addresses it, rather than adding hardware.

blocks.heading: Scale to the Symptom
blocks.body: Slow interactive dashboards point to VizQL capacity. Queued or late refreshes point to the backgrounder.

blocks.heading: Row-Level Security
blocks.body: An entitlements table filtered by the logged-in user, applied on the published data source, so one dashboard serves many audiences.

blocks.heading: Cloud or Self-Managed
blocks.body: Tableau Cloud removes infrastructure work but gives up control of upgrades and topology. Self-managed is the opposite trade.

blocks.heading: High Availability
blocks.body: Redundant processes across several nodes, so a single failure does not stop the platform.

blocks.heading: Content Lifecycle
blocks.body: Use repository usage data to find unused content and retire it. Stale dashboards cost trust as well as resources.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Tableau Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Tableau Architect:

sampleQuestions.question: Extract refreshes are queueing and finishing hours late, while interactive dashboards perform fine. Which capacity should be increased?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The backgrounder runs extract refreshes and subscriptions, so queued refreshes point directly at it.
whyWrong: VizQL renders views, which are performing fine here.
The gateway routes requests and is not the bottleneck described.
The repository stores metadata rather than running refreshes.

sampleQuestions.question: Each regional manager must see only their own region's rows, but the business wants one dashboard for everyone. What should the architect implement?
options: Row-level security using an entitlements table on the published data source
A quick filter set to each region
sampleQuestions.explanation: Row-level security filters rows by the logged-in user, so one dashboard safely serves every region.
whyWrong: Separate sites is a heavy structure for a row-level requirement.
One workbook per region multiplies maintenance and still risks mistakes.
A filter can be changed by the user, so it is not a security control.

sampleQuestions.question: Interactive dashboards are slow at month end when hundreds of users log in at once, while refreshes complete on time. What should be scaled?
sampleQuestions.explanation: VizQL renders views for interactive users, so concurrency problems during viewing point to it.
whyWrong: Backgrounder handles refreshes, which are fine in this scenario.
Storage size does not address rendering concurrency.
Projects are an organisational structure, not a performance lever.

sampleQuestions.question: A company wants Tableau without managing servers, patching or upgrade windows. Which option fits, and what is the trade-off?
options: Tableau Cloud, giving up control of infrastructure and upgrade timing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tableau Cloud removes infrastructure work but means Salesforce controls the platform and when it is upgraded.
whyWrong: Desktop is an authoring tool, not a sharing platform.
Self-managed is the option that requires exactly the work they want to avoid.
Prep prepares data and does not host content.

sampleQuestions.question: Every team reports a different figure for the same measure. What is the architectural fix?
options: A certified published data source with the agreed definition, reused by all
sampleQuestions.explanation: One governed, certified source with the agreed calculation stops teams defining the same measure differently.
whyWrong: Licences do not affect definitions.
Training does not prevent definitions drifting apart again.
Reconciliation treats the symptom every month.

sampleQuestions.question: Which component stores users, permissions, metadata and usage history?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The repository is the PostgreSQL database holding the platform's own metadata, including usage history.
whyWrong: VizQL renders visualisations.
The gateway routes incoming requests.
The data engine stores and queries extract data.

sampleQuestions.question: An extract takes too long to refresh. What should be tried before adding hardware?
options: Filter rows, remove unused fields and aggregate the extract
Switch every workbook to live connections
sampleQuestions.explanation: Most refresh problems are caused by extracts that are larger than they need to be, and reducing them is cheaper than scaling.
whyWrong: More frequent refreshes of a slow extract makes it worse.
Hardware should follow content optimisation, not precede it.
Live connections move load onto the source database.

sampleQuestions.question: How should permissions be granted in a large deployment?
options: To groups, at the project level
By exporting content to PDF for those without access
sampleQuestions.explanation: Group permissions set on projects scale as people and content change, and new content inherits sensible access.
whyWrong: Per-user, per-workbook permissions become unmanageable.
Shared accounts remove accountability.
PDF exports bypass governance and go stale.

sampleQuestions.question: What does certifying a data source do?
options: Marks it as reviewed and trusted so users prefer it over ad-hoc sources
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certification is a governance signal that helps users pick the trusted source.
whyWrong: It does not change refresh performance.
Certification is not an encryption feature.
Certified sources are intended for broad use.

sampleQuestions.question: How can an architect find dashboards that nobody uses?
options: Check the size of each workbook
Analyse usage data from the repository
Delete anything older than a year
sampleQuestions.explanation: The repository records views and usage, which is the reliable way to identify content to retire.
whyWrong: File size says nothing about usage.
Surveys are slow and incomplete.
Age alone does not indicate value: some old dashboards are heavily used.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a highly available Tableau Server deployment require?
sampleQuestions.explanation: High availability comes from redundancy: multiple nodes running the key processes so one failure does not stop the platform.
whyWrong: Extracts are unrelated to availability.
Backups allow recovery but not continuous availability.
One big server remains a single point of failure.

sampleQuestions.question: A live connection to the warehouse is causing heavy load every time users open dashboards. The data only changes nightly. What should change?
options: Use a scheduled extract refreshed after the nightly load
Move to a larger warehouse instance
Ask users to open dashboards less often
sampleQuestions.explanation: If the source only changes nightly, an extract gives the same currency with far less load on the warehouse.
whyWrong: Upgrading the warehouse pays for a problem that an extract removes.
More rendering capacity does not reduce source database load.
Restricting usage defeats the purpose of the platform.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main risk of building one workbook per audience instead of using row-level security?
options: Maintenance multiplies and the copies drift apart
sampleQuestions.explanation: Duplicated workbooks must each be updated for every change, and they inevitably diverge.
whyWrong: Rendering speed is not the central issue.
Permissions are still required on every copy.
More copies means more refresh work, not less.

sampleQuestions.question: Which structure should projects reflect?
options: The file size of each workbook
The alphabetical order of workbook names
sampleQuestions.explanation: Projects aligned to business structure let group permissions be set once and inherited by new content.
whyWrong: Creation date does not reflect who should see what.
Size is irrelevant to organisation.
Alphabetical grouping carries no access meaning.

sampleQuestions.question: A dashboard contains twelve worksheets and nine quick filters, and is slow. What is the most likely cause?
options: Each worksheet and filter issues queries, so the dashboard is doing too much work
sampleQuestions.explanation: Every worksheet and filter on a dashboard generates queries, so heavily loaded dashboards are slow regardless of hardware.
whyWrong: Row-level security has a cost but is not the main factor with this much content.
Certification is a label and has no performance cost.
Disk space rarely causes this pattern.
